Dig or No-Dig
Choosing your approach
Both methods can grow a good crop. The useful question is which suits your ground, your compost supply and the amount of work you can manage. You can change your mind as the garden develops.
Turn soil and mix in compost.
Leave soil intact; compost on top.
No need to turn the ground.
Still needs organic matter over time.
New beds need plenty of compost.
Cardboard for a new weedy bed.
Does not cure every wet site.
No annual turning of the soil.
Still weed, water and top up compost.
My own beds have taken both routes: digging first and changing to no-dig, or starting over lawn. Choose for your plot. In either system, work from paths to avoid treading the beds.

GROWING TECHNIQUES · CULTIVATION

Dig or No-Dig
Choosing your approach

Both methods can grow a good crop. The useful question is which suits your ground, your compost supply and the amount of work you can manage. You can change your mind as the garden develops.

Digging

Turn soil and mix in compost.

No-dig

Leave soil intact; compost on top.

What are the trade-offs?
Dig pro	Dig con	No-dig pro	No-dig con
Loosens soil; exposes buried debris.	Hard physical work.	No need to turn the ground.	Compost still needs shifting.
Lets you remove weed roots.	Brings buried weed seeds up.	Mulch smothers many weeds.	Persistent weeds need follow-up.
Can start with less compost.	Still needs organic matter over time.	Feeds soil from the surface.	New beds need plenty of compost.
Uses familiar hand tools.	Requires a spade or fork.	Permanent bed sides are optional.	Cardboard for a new weedy bed.
Can relieve compaction.	Cannot fix every drainage problem.	Leaves soil structure intact.	Does not cure every wet site.
Can switch to no-dig later.	Repeated digging disturbs soil life.	No annual turning of the soil.	Still weed, water and top up compost.
You needn’t join a camp

My own beds have taken both routes: digging first and changing to no-dig, or starting over lawn. Choose for your plot. In either system, work from paths to avoid treading the beds.

THE VEGETABLE GURU · DRAFT
IMPERIAL · 149

blocks.text: Here we are starting a small bed over grass or ordinary weeds. On an existing weed-free bed, you can leave out the cardboard and add compost straight to the surface.
You need: Plain brown cardboard, well-rotted compost, rake, watering can and a trowel. A barrow saves carrying.

Mark out a bed you can reach from the paths. Remove tape and staples from plain cardboard, then overlap the sheets generously so light cannot get through the joins. Wet dry cardboard to help it lie flat. Clear woody growth and rubbish first.

Spread about 4 inches of well-rotted compost over the cardboard. Break up lumps, remove woody pieces and firm gently with the back of a rake. Leave the soil underneath alone. Timber sides are optional; sloping edges will do.

You can plant straight into the finished layer when the season suits your crop. For small seeds, use a little finer compost in the drill. Follow the crop’s guide for depth and spacing, and water in. Keep an eye out for weeds pushing through.

Add roughly 1–2 inches of compost each year when the bed is free. Pull small weeds promptly, stop grass creeping in at the edges and water when needed. No-dig saves turning the soil; it doesn’t do the rest of the gardening for you.
Persistent weeds may need repeated clearing or longer under cover. Fresh plant waste shelters slugs; use well-rotted compost. Investigate persistent waterlogging before you start.

blocks.text: Single digging turns the topsoil to one spade’s depth. Use it on a cleared, workable plot; badly compacted ground needs more preparation than this short method can provide.
You need: A digging spade or fork, rake and well-rotted compost. A barrow or sheet holds the first soil you lift.

Remove turf, rubbish and persistent weed roots. Spread well-rotted compost where the soil needs organic matter. Dig a trench across one end, one spade wide and deep. Put this first soil aside; you will need it to fill the final gap.

Turn the next strip of topsoil into the open trench, mixing in the compost. Break large clods and pick out weed roots as you go. Repeat along the bed, keeping the lower subsoil underneath. Fill the last trench with the soil you saved.

Allow loosened soil to settle, then rake the surface level. For small seeds, break the top into fine crumbs. Sow or plant at the depth, spacing and time given in the crop’s guide. Water in, then keep on top of the new weeds.

Keep feeding the soil with compost and cultivate only where needed. Permanent paths help prevent compaction. If the bed becomes easy to work, try leaving it alone and adding compost on top. There is no need to dig simply because it is autumn.

Wait if soil is wet and sticky or frozen. Take small bites and regular breaks. Deep compaction or persistent waterlogging needs separate attention; neither a quick dig nor a compost dressing is a guaranteed cure.
John’s Hackriculture manuscript and videos; RHS and Charles Dowding. Full sources accompany this draft. Diagrams are schematic.
